Patrick Flynn's birthplace is disputed between two U.S. census records (Ireland) and his 1908 death certificate (Pennsylvania). The fact matters because it bears directly on Patrick's origins as an Irish immigrant and on identifying his parents, which is the subject of q_001.

The 1850 U.S. Census (src_001, a_002) lists Patrick, age 5, born in Ireland, in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. The 1860 U.S. Census (src_003, a_009) lists Patrick, age 15, again born in Ireland, in the same Thomas Flynn household. Both records were created by enumerators who visited the household and solicited information from a household member — almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife, who as Patrick's parents would have had direct knowledge of his birth. The 1908 death certificate (src_004, a_012) states Patrick was born in Pennsylvania; this information was provided by James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, identified as the personal-details informant on the certificate.

The two census records are more reliable on this fact. The census informants reported within five to fifteen years of the birth, with direct parental knowledge. Two independently enumerated occasions agree on Ireland. The death certificate informant, James Brown, was not present at Patrick's birth and is reporting a secondhand belief sixty-three years after the event. A son-in-law's recollection of his father-in-law's origins, offered from hearsay decades after the birth, is substantially less reliable than parental reports made while the subject was still a child.

The discrepancy reflects a well-documented historical pattern of immigration-origin confusion (see historical-contradictions.md). James Brown, reporting in 1908, knew Patrick Flynn exclusively as a Pennsylvanian: Patrick had lived in Schuylkill County for the better part of six decades. Brown likely had no firsthand experience of the family's Irish origins — Patrick had immigrated as an infant or very young child, and by the time Brown married into the family, 'Pennsylvania' was simply where the Flynns were from. When the death certificate clerk asked for the birthplace, Brown's only frame of reference was American. He supplied the place he associated with the Flynn family — Pennsylvania — rather than the country Patrick was actually born in. This is the immigration-origin confusion pattern: a secondary informant conflates the decedent's long-established American home with the actual birthplace, particularly when the informant had no exposure to the immigrant generation's arrival story.
